descriptor.assumptions: Assumes OH mole fraction in the normalized gel is a faithful proxy for effective mineralizing base strength, i.e., other cations are not deprotonating/protonating OH pools in ways that decouple the ratio from real alkalinity; ignores buffering by OSDA hydroxide vs. inorganic bases and the contribution of fluoride as an alternative mineralizer; a 1e-6 constant is added because pure-silica gels without Si in the normalized sum are impossible but numerically Si can be extremely small; does not distinguish NaOH from TPAOH hydroxide sources.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases, predictions should shift toward low-density small-pore frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA) and, at very high values, toward Failed via excessive dissolution; as it decreases toward zero, predictions should shift toward high-silica large-pore or 1D frameworks (MFI, MTW, TON, *BEA) and dense phases.
descriptor.falsification: If model performance does not change relative to a run with a permuted version of this column, or if observed phase boundaries in validation recipes do not align with OH/Si (e.g., LTA forming at low OH/Si and MFI at high OH/Si in held-out publications), the hypothesis is contradicted.
descriptor.hypothesis: The hydroxide-to-silicon ratio (gel alkalinity per framework-forming Si) is a master variable steering which framework crystallizes: high alkalinity accelerates nucleation of low-density, small-pore frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA, AEL), while low alkalinity or near-neutral fluoride-type conditions favor high-silica, large-pore or one-dimensional frameworks (MFI, MTW, TON, *BEA) and can push systems toward dense/quartz phases or Failed when dissolution is too slow.
descriptor.mechanism: Hydroxide concentration controls the dissolution rate of amorphous aluminosilicate/silicate precursors, the steady-state concentration of soluble anionic silicate and aluminate oligomers, and the nucleation rate. At high OH/Si, abundant small oligomers and high supersaturation promote metastable, low-framework-density phases with many small cages (LTA, FAU, CHA); at low OH/Si, dissolution is slow and condensation is favored over hydrolysis, stabilizing denser or higher-silica frameworks (MFI, MTW, TON) or quartz/dense products. Because tree ensembles split one column at a time, this emergent ratio is invisible to the current D0 features even though both OH and Si are individually present.
descriptor.name: hydroxide_per_tetrahedral_si

descriptor.assumptions: The conformer volume approximates the effective packing volume of the OSDA in the pore; a single conformer is representative (flexible OSDAs may adopt smaller in-pore volumes); formal charge equals the templating charge (no partial compensation by hydroxide/water); only OSDA1 is considered even when n_osda > 1; when no OSDA is present the descriptor is ~0 and its interpretation as 'very bulky low-charge' is only a crude proxy.
descriptor.expected_effect: As osda_charge_density increases, outcomes shift toward small-pore, cage-based, higher framework-charge frameworks (LTA, CHA, AEI, LEV, AEL) and away from large-pore, channel-type high-silica frameworks (MFI, MTW, *BEA, MWW, UTL); values near zero (bulky or absent OSDA) increase the probability of Failed or dense products.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out publications show high-charge-density OSDAs (e.g., small dialkylammonium ions) crystallizing MFI or *BEA, or very bulky low-charge OSDAs producing CHA/LTA, the descriptor does not carry the hypothesized phase-selection information and should be dropped.
descriptor.hypothesis: The formal charge of the OSDA per unit of its molecular volume (charge density) steers which framework crystallizes: compact, high-charge-density cations stabilize frameworks with many small cages and high framework charge density (LTA, CHA, AEI, LEV, AEL), while bulky, low-charge-density cations template large-pore or high-silica frameworks with wide channels (*BEA, MFI, MTW, MWW, UTL) and very low charge density approaches OSDA-free (Failed or dense) regimes.
descriptor.mechanism: Each framework framework negative charge (from Al or other heteroatom tetrahedra) must be balanced by an OSDA charge located inside a pore or cage. A cation with high charge concentrated in a small volume can pack efficiently into small cages and stabilize low-framework-density, small-ring structures with high charge per cell; a large cation with sparse charge occupies open channel systems where the charge-to-space demand is low. The volume normalizes away simple size so the descriptor captures how much compensating framework charge the OSDA demands per unit pore space it fills, a quantity a tree ensemble cannot form by splitting on charge or volume alone.

descriptor.assumptions: The mole-fraction ratio is a proxy for the effective T-atom concentration and water activity; it ignores other solvents (e.g., ethylene glycol), seed addition, and whether water is added post-gelation. Summing only Si, Al, P, Ge, Ga, B approximates framework-forming species and omits heteroatoms (Ti, Zn, Zr, etc.) that can enter frameworks in specific chemistries. The additive 1e-6 constants prevent division by zero but slightly distort near-zero compositions.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases (more concentrated gel): probability of open, cage-based frameworks (FAU, LTA, CHA, AEI, LEV) should decrease, while MFI, MEL, TON, MTW, FER, MOR, dense phases and Failed should increase; at very high values Failed should dominate from water-starved polymerization. At very low values Failure should also increase due to nucleation starvation, with an intermediate window favoring open frameworks.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out recipes show that cage-based frameworks such as FAU or LTA crystallize just as readily at high T-atom/water ratios as at low ones, or that the descriptor carries negligible split importance and does not change predictions on unseen publications, the hypothesis is contradicted.
descriptor.hypothesis: The concentration of framework-forming T atoms (Si, Al, P, Ge, Ga, B) relative to water in the gel steers which framework crystallizes: dilute gels (low ratio, high water) favor low-framework-density, open frameworks with cages or large cages (FAU, LTA, CHA, AEI, LEV) but risk Failure from slow nucleation, while concentrated gels (high ratio, low water) favor denser, high-silica or medium/large-pore frameworks (MFI, MEL, TON, MTW, FER, MOR) and, at the extreme, dense phases or amorphous Failure because oligomer condensation outpaces restructuring.
descriptor.mechanism: Water is both the solvent and the medium controlling hydrolysis, dissolution of amorphous precursor, and the chemical potential of silicate/aluminate/phosphate oligomers. At high dilution, monomer and small-oligomer activities are low, nucleation is slow, and only frameworks with low framework density (open, cage-based, high void volume per T atom) that can grow under low supersaturation are thermodynamically competitive. At low dilution, high T-atom activity promotes rapid polymerization and nucleation of frameworks with high framework density and dense or 1D-channel structures; water-starved gels also have reduced mobility, favoring metastable dense phases or incomplete crystallization (Failed). Tree models can split directly on this ratio column, which is not a monotone transform of any single D0 column.
descriptor.name: framework_species_water_ratio
